newsitem.title: TURKEY: Kurdish party leaders jailed in Turkish flag case.
newsitem.headline: Kurdish party leaders jailed in Turkish flag case.

text.p: A Turkish court on Wednesday jailed the leadership of the country's main Kurdish party for aiding separatist rebels in a case that could damage Turkey's relations with the West.
Ankara State Security Court convicted 31 leading members of the People's Democratic Party (HADEP) and sentenced them to between 4-1/2 and six years in prison.
But a far heavier punishment -- 22-1/2 years in jail -- was meted out to a youth who tore down a Turkish flag at a HADEP congress last June, precipitating the case against the Kurdish party leaders.
"A close link was discovered between HADEP and the illegal terror organisation PKK," judge Orhan Karadeniz told the court.

Party leader Murat Bozlak and another party member were jailed for six years. The case was brought after Faysal Akcan tore down the Turkish flag and replaced it with a banner of the Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK) rebels.
The flag incident outraged many Turks and led to counter protests throughout the country.
Twenty-nine other HADEP members were sentenced to 4-1/2 years and 14 other defendants were found not guilty.
A HADEP official among those acquitted said Bozlak was abroad and had not returned for the verdict.
"We were in Vienna for talks and the chairman is still there. He is expected back in a few days," leading HADEP member Sirri Sakik told Reuters at the party's headquarters.
Party deputy leader Osman Ozcelik told a news conference the case was designed to suppress Turkey's Kurdish minority.

"The aim was to silence HADEP, which has become the voice of those who are crushed, who are exploited, who are repressed who favour democracy," said Ozcelik. "The aim was oppression and intimidation of Kurds."
The case may damage Turkey's human rights image abroad. "It will be further evidence for those who believe Turkey is a long way from meeting standards on human rights," a Western diplomat said.
Ankara's efforts to join the European Union have been hindered by human rights criticism, as well as economic problems and disputes with neighbour Greece.
HADEP, which does not advocate violence or outright separatism, was formed in 1994 after another pro-Kurdish party was banned and six of its MPs were jailed for links to the guerrillas.
The prosecutor said during the 10-month HADEP trial that the party was used as a front to recruit Kurdish fighters to take part in the rebel war in southeast Turkey.
He also said news reports from a Kurdish news agency close to the rebels found in HADEP's headquarters were evidence of the politicians' connivance with the guerrillas.
More than 24,000 people have died in Turkey and neighbouring northern Iraq in almost 13 years of conflict between the guerrillas and Turkish security forces.
The judge said he would ask the chief prosecutor's office to investigate HADEP in a move that could lead to the party's closure by the constitutional court.
Ozcelik said the party would not take closure lying down.
"We will not give up this place. Even if HADEP is closed new parties will be formed," he said.
